heading: When profit grows, review cash commitments before choosing a tax strategy
body:
A profitable year can create several competing uses for the same cash: payroll, estimated taxes, equipment, debt principal, owner spending, and an operating reserve. Start the planning conversation with those commitments on one dated schedule. A tax idea is easier to evaluate when the owner can see what it costs, when funds leave the business, and who must complete the work.

For a fictional business with $500,000 of projected profit, neither that profit figure nor the bank balance establishes the amount available for a discretionary purchase. Receivables may not be collected yet, debt payments consume cash, and owner-level tax payments may occur outside the company books. Ask the adviser to reconcile the company forecast with the owner’s projection before comparing strategies.

Bring current financial statements, prior returns, payroll records, ownership information, and a list of decisions with real deadlines. For each recommendation, request the eligibility facts, implementation steps, expected cash effect, filing responsibility, and follow-up date. Separate an illustrative estimate from an implemented result. The most useful plan explains what to do next and how completion will be verified.
